original_question: A positive integer is called a pseudo-cube of third kind if some nontrivial permutation of its decimal digits is a perfect cube. Among those numbers, are there infinitely many that are themselves perfect cubes?
target_in_paper: The exact target is item 91, "Pseudo-Cubes of Third Kind": "Question: How many pseudo-cubes of third kind are cubes? (We conjecture: an infinity)." This is the nearest official formulation in the paper and matches your draft directly. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper: it uses the paper’s object "pseudo-cube of third kind," keeps the decimal-digit permutation setting, and asks the same infinitude question about those numbers that are themselves perfect cubes. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
missing_details: The ambient domain should be stated explicitly as positive integers written in base 10; this is implicit in the paper’s digit-permutation sequences. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

In the paper’s usage, "nontrivial permutation" means a permutation different from the identity permutation; this is spelled out explicitly for the same "third kind" terminology in item 83. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

To be fully paper-faithful, the definition should allow a nonidentity permutation of digit positions even when repeated digits make the written numeral unchanged; the inclusion of 343 in item 91 strongly indicates that convention. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The examples 10 and 100 in item 91 show that permutations producing leading zeros are intended to count, with the permuted digit string read as the corresponding decimal integer (for example, 01 = 1). This is an inference from the listed terms rather than a verbatim definition. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The paper phrases the problem as a counting question together with the explicit conjecture that the answer is infinite, so a stand-alone rewrite should preserve that infinitude framing. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
The cube question is also the m = 3 specialization of the paper’s general item 94 on pseudo-m-powers of third kind. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
refined_question: Let n be a positive integer written in base 10. Call n a pseudo-cube of third kind if there exists a nonidentity permutation of its digit positions such that the resulting decimal numeral is a perfect cube, with leading zeros created by the permutation allowed and with repeated digits permitted to yield the same numeral. Are there infinitely many perfect cubes n that are pseudo-cubes of third kind? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: This is exactly the m = 3 case of item 94: are there infinitely many pseudo-m-powers of third kind that are themselves m-powers, specialized to m = 3? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
justification: The paper is a catalog of numbered sequences and open questions, not a theorem-style article with labels such as Conjecture 1.1 or Theorem 1.3. After checking the introduction and the nearby numbered items, item 91 is the exact paper statement that your draft is trying to capture. Item 89 gives the baseline first-kind definition (including the identity permutation), item 91 states the cube problem and conjectures infinitude, item 94 gives the explicit m-power generalization, and item 83 clarifies that "nontrivial permutation" means "different from the identity permutation." The only real gaps in your draft are the paper’s implicit conventions revealed by the examples: leading-zero permutations are evidently allowed because 10 and 100 are listed, and repeated-digit swaps appear to count even when the numeral is unchanged, as suggested by the inclusion of 343. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
